Your website does a job for your business: it builds trust, brings in enquiries, takes bookings or sells products. The right website is the one built for that job. Pick the wrong type and you pay for features you never use, or miss the ones that would bring in customers. This guide walks you through the main types of business website, how to choose between them, and what to plan for before you start.

Start with one question: what should your website do?

Before you think about colours, page builders or platforms, decide the main goal. Most business websites have one primary job:

  • Build trust – show who you are, what you do and why people should choose you.
  • Get enquiries – turn visitors into calls, emails, WhatsApp messages or form submissions.
  • Sell online – let customers browse products and pay without talking to you.
  • Take bookings – let clients pick a time and book a service or appointment.
  • Share expertise – publish articles and guides that bring in visitors from Google.

Once the main goal is clear, the right type of website usually picks itself.

The 6 main types of business website

1. Brochure website

A small site with a homepage, about, services and contact page. It works like a digital business card: perfect for trades, consultants and local businesses that mostly get work from referrals and just need to look credible online.

2. Lead generation website

The most common choice for service businesses. Every page is designed to get people to take action: clear service pages, reviews, strong calls to action and a simple contact form or WhatsApp button. A good example is a plumbing business website that turns local searches into booked jobs.

3. E-commerce store

If you sell products, you need an online store with product pages, a cart, secure payments and shipping. On WordPress this is usually built with WooCommerce, which keeps your store fully under your control with no platform fees on every sale.

4. Booking website

Salons, clinics, coaches and consultants often need clients to choose a time slot and pay a deposit online. A booking website connects your calendar to your site so appointments happen without back-and-forth emails.

5. Portfolio website

For designers, photographers, builders and agencies, the work sells itself. A portfolio site puts real projects front and centre, with short case studies that explain the problem, the solution and the result.

6. Content-led website

Some businesses grow mainly through Google. A content-led site combines service pages with a blog of helpful guides, so people find you while researching a problem and then hire you to solve it.

How to choose: a quick checklist

  1. Write down the one action you most want visitors to take.
  2. List the pages you need for that action (for most businesses: home, services, about, reviews, contact).
  3. Decide if you need extras now – online payments, bookings, a member area – or later.
  4. Check who will update the site. If it is you, it must be easy to edit without a developer.
  5. Set a realistic budget and timeline before you ask for quotes.

Why WordPress fits most businesses

WordPress is flexible enough for every type above. You can start with a simple brochure site and add a store, bookings or a blog later without starting again. You own the site and its content, and with a modern builder like Bricks, Oxygen or Etch it stays fast and easy to edit. Be careful with sites generated in seconds by AI tools: they often look fine but are hard for you to change later. I explain why in this article on AI-built websites.

Budget and timeline

Most small and medium business websites fall between $500 and $5,000, depending on the number of pages, features and integrations. A typical business site takes 2–4 weeks from the first call to launch. If money is tight, read how to build a website on a small budget. If you run a bigger company with many teams and integrations, see building a website for a large business. Launching something new? Follow the step-by-step guide for a new business website.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Choosing a platform before deciding what the website must do.
  • Paying for an online store when you only need enquiries.
  • Skipping mobile design – most visitors will see your site on a phone.
  • Launching without basic SEO: page titles, descriptions and a sitemap.
  • Ending up with a site you cannot edit yourself, or don't fully own.

Frequently asked questions

What type of website does a small business need?

Most small businesses start with a lead generation website: a clear homepage, service pages, reviews and an easy way to get in touch. Add online booking or a store only when you actually need it.

Is WordPress good for a business website?

Yes. WordPress powers a large share of the web, is easy to edit, has tools for SEO, booking and e-commerce, and you own the site and its content outright.

How long does it take to build a business website?

A typical business website takes 2–4 weeks from the first call to launch. A simple landing page can be ready in days, while a large store or custom build can take longer.

Can I add an online store later?

Yes. If the site is built on WordPress, you can add WooCommerce later without rebuilding the whole website, so you can start simple and grow.

Conclusion

The right website for your business is the one designed around a single clear goal, built on a platform you own and can edit, and ready to grow when you need more. Start with the job your website has to do, choose the type that matches it, and add features as your business grows. If you would like help choosing or building it, tell me about your project and I'll suggest the right setup with a clear, fixed quote. You can also see websites I have built.

For a small business, the website is often the first impression a customer gets. A good small business website designer turns that first visit into a call, a booking or a sale. A poor one leaves you with a site that looks fine but brings in nothing. This guide explains what a small business website designer actually does, what to look for when hiring one, and the questions to ask before you sign anything.

What does a small business website designer do?

A website designer plans, designs and usually builds your site so it fits your business, not a generic template. A good designer will:

  • Learn about your business, customers and goals before designing anything.
  • Plan the pages and the path visitors take to contact or buy from you.
  • Design a layout that matches your brand and works on phones, tablets and desktops.
  • Build the site so it loads fast and is set up for search engines.
  • Hand it over with training and access, so you can make changes yourself.

Why hire a designer instead of DIY?

Website builders make it easy to put pages online, but they don't tell you what to say, how to structure the site, or why visitors leave without contacting you. A designer brings that experience. You save the hours you would spend learning tools, avoid common mistakes, and launch sooner with a site that is built to bring in customers, not just to exist.

7 things to look for in a small business website designer

1. Real, live websites in their portfolio

Mockups are easy. Ask to see live websites they have launched for real businesses, and click through them on your phone. See my recent work for an example of what to ask for.

2. Mobile-first design

Most of your visitors will arrive on a phone. The designer should show you the mobile version early, not as an afterthought.

3. Speed and SEO built in

A beautiful site that loads slowly or can't be found on Google won't help you. Look for clean builds, optimised images, proper page titles, descriptions and a sitemap from day one.

4. A site you can edit and own

You should get full admin access and be able to change text and images yourself. Avoid setups that lock you into the designer for every small change. Sites generated in seconds by AI tools often have this problem; here is why clients still can’t edit AI-built websites.

5. A clear process and fixed quote

Good designers explain each step, agree a timeline and give a fixed price that lists what is included, such as pages, revisions and features, before any work starts.

6. Support after launch

Things come up after go-live: new pages, updates, small fixes. Ask what support is included and how quickly they respond.

7. Honest reviews

Read reviews on independent platforms like Upwork or Google, not just quotes on their own site. Look for comments about communication, deadlines and results.

Questions to ask before hiring

  1. Can I see three live websites you built for businesses like mine?
  2. What exactly is included in the price, and what costs extra?
  3. How many revisions do I get, and how long will the project take?
  4. Will I own the website and have full admin access?
  5. How will you make the site fast and ready for Google?
  6. What happens if I need help after launch?

How much does it cost?

Most small business websites cost between $500 and $5,000, depending on pages, features and how custom the design is. A simple brochure site sits at the lower end; a site with bookings or an online store costs more. If you are working with a tight budget, read how to build a website on a small budget, and if you are still deciding what you need, see how to choose the right website for your business.

Red flags to watch out for

  • No live examples, only mockups or templates.
  • Vague pricing with no list of what is included.
  • No mention of mobile, speed or SEO.
  • The designer keeps ownership of your domain, hosting or login.
  • Slow or unclear replies before you have even hired them.

Frequently asked questions

How much does a small business website designer cost?

Most small business websites cost between $500 and $5,000, depending on the number of pages, features and how much custom design you need. Always ask for a fixed quote that lists what is included.

How long does it take to design a small business website?

Usually 2–4 weeks from the first call to launch for a typical small business site. Smaller one-page sites can be ready in a few days.

Should I use a freelancer or an agency?

A freelancer is often faster and more affordable, and you talk directly to the person building your site. An agency can suit very large projects that need a bigger team.

Will I be able to edit the website myself?

You should. Ask for a site built on a platform like WordPress with an easy editor, plus full admin access at handover, so you can update text, images and pages without paying for every change.

Conclusion

The right small business website designer understands your customers, designs for phones first, builds a fast site that Google can find, and hands you a website you fully own and can edit. Use the checklist and questions above to compare options with confidence. If you would like a website built this way, tell me about your project and I'll send a clear, fixed quote. To learn more about hiring, see how to choose a freelance website designer.
